It just so happens that Dr. Stockmann co-founded this spa with his brother, Peter Stockmann (Behzad Dabu), who is the town mayor. The mayor believes the spa is crucial to the financial health of the whole community.</p><p>And here lies the central conflict: the spa waters make people sick. In order to solve the problem, and save lives, they must shut down the spa — which will bankrupt the town.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.0" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> “An Enemy of the People” </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b00000" name="module-b00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When</b>: Through June 14<br><b>Where</b>: TimeLine Theatre Company, 5035 N. Broadway<br><b>Info</b>: Tickets start at $62</div> </div><p>Ibsen crafted a straightforward story of individual morality, and he masterfully portrays the difficulty of speaking truth to power in the face of widespread corruption. The storyline offers a stark reminder that human nature hasn’t changed much in the last 100 years as we still see powerful people putting profits before the well being of the public everyday (or at least every time we turn on the news).</p><p>Director Ron OJ Parson has a knack for working with talented ensembles while allowing space for individual performances to shine. Allan is excellent as Dr. Stockmann. He’s truly engaging as his social circle crumbles, and his friends evolve into foes. Dabu portrays a formidable antagonist as the powerful small town politician who, even as villain, truly believes he’s the hero.</p><p>The themes in the play feel more important than ever. But here is where I take my millennial heel turn. Sitting in an audience, where everyone around me is likely a generation older than I am, it feels <i>safe</i>. But I want the opposition to have a stronger voice. I wanted to question the stance I walked into the theater with to maybe dive deeper into my own sensibilities. Here, boundaries are not pushed. No risk is taken. Instead it feels like it expresses ideals that we all already mutually agreed upon.</p><p>That’s because the production offers little in the way of a counterargument. Allan portrays the hero doctor admirably, and at times he’s almost too compelling. As an audience, we are seeing science be attacked in real time in our real lives. This should easily resonate. when his adversaries are morally unequipped to spar with him. In the second act, when Dr. Stockmann presents his argument for spa closure to the town, he easily outwits each character standing in opposition. The staging is clever, and the decision to send actors into the aisles and seats to interact with the audience and pull us in as mock townspeople, adds an appreciated touch.</p><p>But in a show with so much potential to spark larger conversations, there’s no real substance for debate.</p><p>TimeLine has a reputation for staging historical dramas with contemporary connections. This worthwhile show, which argues the importance of free speech and social responsibilities, is a great choice for the inaugural opening. But with flat antagonists, the production comes off a little one-sided: a victory for the “enemy” but less compelling for the audience.</p>

entries.title: Rogers Park man charged in fatal Edgewater shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man faces murder and gun charges in connection with a fatal early-morning Edgewater shooting earlier this week, police announced Saturday.</p><p>Ammar Houssamo, 53, was charged with first-degree murder and aggravated unlawful possession of a weapon, police announced. He was arrested in Evanston shortly after shots rang out in the 1400 block of West Thome around 7:20 a.m. Thursday, police said.</p><p>Houssamo, of Rogers Park, allegedly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/15/dog-walker-fatally-shot-trying-fleeing-gunman-who-then-turned-gun-on-self-in-edgewater-police" >shot a man who was walking his dog</a> before turning the gun on himself, according to Chicago police. The man was pronounced dead at Presence St. Francis Hospital in Evanston.</p><p>Houssamo was taken to the same hospital, where he was in critical condition and arrested by Chicago police later Thursday.</p>

entries.title: U. of C. faculty and parents protest Lab School policy they say limits classroom discussion, inclusion
entries.summary: <p>Students, parents and teachers at a private school run by the University of Chicago are rallying against a policy they say limits what students are exposed to at school and hurts teachers’ ability to support marginalized students.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1775123874/chicagolab/eajqxbdbjw5x84yvf6vw/StandardsforViewpoint-NeutralEducationinSupportofStudent-CenteredOpenInquiry.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>A new policy</u></a> at the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools, which serve around 2,000 students from preschool through high school, establishes “standards for viewpoint-neutral education” and gives teachers guidance on how to handle “contested issues.”</p><p>School administrators say the policy, which had gotten pushback since a draft was first shared in January, is meant to encourage students to become “independent thinkers” and support “open inquiry.”</p><p>“The purpose of viewpoint-neutral education is not to limit inquiry or discourage engagement with difficult, important, or contested topics,” the policy states. “Rather, the goal is to ensure that Lab classrooms and school spaces remain… places where students can encounter, explore, and evaluate important questions without being steered toward or away from particular conclusions by the authority of adults.”</p><p>But dozens of parents, many of whom are faculty at the University of Chicago, say the policy actually restricts conversations in the classroom and could prevent teachers from creating an inclusive environment for students.</p><p>Some faculty members, led by the university’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors, gathered on the school’s Hyde Park campus Friday to <a class="Link" href="https://www.uchicagoaaup.org/statements/lab-school-viewpoint-neutrality" target="_blank" ><u>deliver a petition to administrators opposing the policy</u></a>. Many wore shirts that read “free teachers raise thinkers” and held signs with the phrase “Love is love, neutrality enables hate, let our teachers advocate.”</p><p>“Usually rules that restrict what people can say are called censorship,” Patrick Morrissey, a professor of poetry at U. of C., said at the protest.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Some parents said the policy encourages multiple viewpoints on current events and sticky real-world issues.</p><p>“If you care about diversity, you should be delighted that there’s an emphasis now on diversity of viewpoints,” a parent who declined to be named told the Maroon.</p><p>The policy says teachers are allowed to take a stance on “widely settled historical judgments,” like denouncing slavery and the Holocaust, but taking a position on current debates is discouraged.</p><p>A “frequently asked questions” document related to the policy identifies several “active areas of disagreement in contemporary public debate” where teachers should remain neutral, including abortion, immigration laws and enforcement, policing and climate policy.</p><p>The policy says Lab School classrooms will still be welcoming to all students, but protesters worry some students’ identities and beliefs are tied up with ongoing political debates, and that could make them feel ostracized.</p><p>For example, some worry the policy is especially difficult for transgender students, as the Trump administration continues to put forward policies that target trans people. Federal officials are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lgbtq/2025/03/25/whats-at-stake-when-feds-investigate-local-accommodations-for-trans-students" target="_blank" ><u>investigating Chicago Public Schools</u></a> for allowing trans students to use the bathroom that aligns with their gender identity and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/04/30/noble-charter-network-suburban-school-districts-face-federal-probe-over-lgbtq-related-lessons" target="_blank" ><u>other schools in Illinois</u></a> over whether parents are allowed to opt out of lessons that talk about gender identity.</p><p>“Let’s be clear that neutrality that refuses to protect vulnerable children is not neutrality at all,” said Michele Friedner, a U. of C. professor who has a transgender child at one of the Lab Schools and felt like her child was already separated from other students when they were made to room with the only other trans student on a school field trip.</p><p>“Think about what this means for a child, for children, to walk into a school and understand that the institution is debating whether you deserve recognition, protection, or dignity at all,” Friedner said.</p><p>The debate at the Lab Schools takes place against the backdrop of the Trump administration’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/03/14/g-s1-53831/dei-universities-education-department-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion</u></a> in K-12 and higher education and efforts to <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2025/07/01/trump-threatens-sex-ed-funding-over-gender-identity-and-trans-youth/" target="_blank" ><u>remove instruction about LGBTQ people</u></a> and themes from school lessons. Some see this policy as similarly controlling classroom conversations.</p><p>“Let’s be clear, that’s what contested issues are: Anything that might upset the Trump administration, its collaborators, and those who wish to curry favor with him,” Morrissey said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" social issues, faculty members raised concerns that a similar policy could be adopted that would more directly affect how they teach. Jessica Darrow, a professor in the university’s Crown School of Social Work, said social justice is central to her work and a neutrality policy could go against her profession’s code of ethics.</p><p>“My students need to be able to learn to take a stand on social issues and not remain value-neutral on issues,” Darrow said.</p><p>Darrow has two sons who’ve attended the Lab Schools. She commended several parts of how the schools work, including their focus on experiential and play-based learning.</p><p>But she thinks administrators are overstepping with this policy.</p><p>Darrow’s younger son is in seventh grade at a Lab School, and he also takes issue with the policy, she said. He appreciates hearing his teachers’ thoughts and feelings during lessons, and he learns more about how to interact with others when his teachers aren’t worried about violating the policy.</p><p>Darrow said her seventh grader saw the policy’s negative effects during a recent classroom conversation about bullying. His teacher explained the difference between a “bystander,” someone who merely observes bullying or other harmful behavior, and an “upstander,” someone who tries to put a stop to it. Darrow’s son told her the teacher stopped short of recommending which path students should take because he didn’t want to be reprimanded for violating the policy.</p><p>“I think that’s where the problem lies,” Darrow said. “The chilling effect of these standards on our teachers’ ability to really do their jobs well.”</p>

entries.title: Hugo Cuypers scores again as Fire blank Montreal
entries.summary: <p>Hugo Cuypers scored his MLS-leading 13th goal this season, Philip Zinckernagel added a goal and an assist, and the Fire beat CF Montreal 2-0 on Saturday at Saputo Stadium in Montreal.</p><p>Cuypers has at least one goal in each games he has played this season and is just the third player in MLS history to score in 10 consecutive regular-season contests.</p><p>Chris Brady had six saves for Chicago and has six shutouts this season.</p><p>The Fire (7-4-2), who beat D.C. United 3-1 on Wednesday to snap a three-game losing streak, have won back-to-back games.</p><p>Zinckernagel ran onto a failed clearance attempt by Brayan Vera and skipped a first-touch shot from just inside the top of the penalty box into the net to open the scoring in the 14th minute.</p><p>Thomas Gillier had four saves for Montreal (4-8-1).</p><p>The Fire beat Montreal 3-0 at Soldier Field on Feb. 28.<br></p>

entries.title: The Cubs' Caleb Thielbar pitches scoreless inning in rehab assignment
entries.summary: <p><b>Caleb Thielbar </b>made his first rehab appearance Saturday afternoon in Appleton, Wisconsin, pitching for High Class A South Bend against the Wisconsin Timber Rattlers, who are in the Brewers’ system.</p><p>If the Cubs were hoping to see how the left-handed reliever, who’s recovering from a strained left hamstring, responded to a high-leverage situation, they were disappointed.</p><p>South Bend held a 19-run lead when Thielbar entered in the eighth. He pitched a scoreless inning, allowing a single, walking one and striking out two. The final score was 24-4.</p><p>Manager <b>Craig Counsell </b>said Thielbar was expected to rejoin the team Sunday — unless, he joked, Thielbar elected to spend the night in Appleton for the complimentary breakfast at the Best Western.</p><p>Thielbar, 39, who was drafted by the Brewers in the 18th round in 2009, spent the 2010 season with the Timber Rattlers. Even then, he was used exclusively in relief.</p><p>In 10 seasons spanning 425 appearances in the big leagues — the first eight with the Twins, the last two with the Cubs — he has never made a start.</p><p>In eight appearances this season for the Cubs, Thielbar has two saves in injured <b>Daniel Palencia’s </b>absence and also was credited with two wins.</p><p>Thielbar signed a one-year deal for $4.5 million with the Cubs. He almost certainly will be activated for the Brewers series that starts Monday. If the Cubs elect to keep only two lefties in the pen, <b>Ryan Rolison </b>appears the most likely to be optioned.</p><p><b>Home-running</b></p><p>The Cubs did not hit a home run Friday and have hit only two in their last six games, <b>Alex Bregman </b>and <b>Ian Happ </b>going deep in Atlanta. They’re 5-9 in games in which they do not homer, 24-7 when they do. The most home runs the Cubs have hit in a game in Rate Field is five, which they’ve done twice, the last time on Sept. 25, 2020, when <b>Willson Contreras </b>hit two, and <b>Kyle Schwarber</b>, <b>Javy Baez </b>and <b>Victor Caratini </b>hit one apiece.</p><p>Cubs pitchers allowed three home runs in a game Friday for only the sixth time this season. White Sox shortstop <b>Colson Montgomery </b>took <b>Edward Cabrera </b>deep for his 12th home run in the second inning, <b>Miguel Vargas </b>took Rolison deep in the sixth for his 10th home run and <b>Jarred Kelenic </b>hit his first of the season off <b>Javier Assad </b>in the ninth. All three home runs came with the bases empty.</p><p><b>Waiter, there’s a golf ball in my soup</b></p><p>Counsell told a story Saturday afternoon from his playing days when he was with the Diamondbacks. In one visiting clubhouse, Counsell said without mentioning names, there was a cook famous for the chili he served the players.</p><p>“It was good,’’ Counsell said. “That’s what everybody ate, the chili.’’</p><p>The players suspected, however, that cleanliness didn’t rank particularly high with this cook. So before they left town, knowing they would be back two weeks later, one of the players dropped a golf ball in the pot.</p><p>“The next time we came back,’’ Counsell said. “The golf ball was still there.’’</p><p>After that, Counsell said, the cook placed the golf ball on top of a chili bowl. From then on, he said, it was called “Golf Ball Chili.’’</p><table class="cf wS" role="presentation" style="border-collapse: collapse;" id="rte-838b6020-517c-11f1-94f2-b3262fa974f7"><tbody><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amq" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px 16px; vertical-align: top; width: 44px; visibility: hidden;"></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amr" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px; width: 698.667px;"></td></tr></tbody></table>

entries.title: Versatile Sean Newcomb a valuable piece of White Sox bullpen
entries.summary: <p>A pitcher like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> reliever <b>Sean Newcomb </b>gives a manager options. The Sox’ <b>Will Venable </b>can call on Newcomb less regularly for longer outings that eat up innings, or more commonly for shorter appearances.</p><p>Either way, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/15/sean-newcomb-to-bullpen-mike-vasil-exits-start-saturday-with-right-elbow-soreness" >Newcomb brings an important ingredient</a> to the Sox bullpen.</p><p>“[Newcomb’s] versatility is huge,” Venable said before Saturday’s game against the Cubs. “Having the performance be what it is as well is a really valuable piece to have.”</p><p>Venable brings up a good point. A pitcher’s adaptability doesn’t have much value if he isn’t getting batters out. Newcomb is producing.</p><p>Entering Saturday, Newcomb had a 2.81 ERA in 19 appearances and hadn’t allowed an earned run in his last eight. Eleven of his appearances have been more than an inning, including six of at least two.</p><p>As for his usage, Newcomb has appeared on consecutive days four times but only once since April 12.</p><p>“We’ll see what it looks like at the end of the year, but just knowing that he can go shorter spurts more frequently or longer distance less frequently is a good thing to have,” Venable said.</p><p>Newcomb, 32, is in his first season with the Sox, after signing a one-year, $4.5-million contract in December.</p><p><b>Making moves</b></p><p>Before Saturday’s game, the Sox acquired minor-league outfielder <b>Junior Perez </b>from the Athletics for minor-league left-hander <b>Jackson Nove</b>. Perez was optioned to Triple-A Charlotte and added to the Sox’ 40-man roster.</p><p>Venable provided a detailed scouting report on Perez, 24, who was designated for assignment Thursday by the Athletics after hitting .210 over 36 games with Triple-A Las Vegas. Perez hits lefties well and is athletic but strikes out a lot.</p><p>Last season, he showed more at the plate, despite striking out 165 times. Between Double- and Triple-A, Perez had a .348 on-base percentage and stole 27 bases.</p><p>“At his floor, a really good defender that can run the bases,” Venable said. “A really good athlete.”</p><p>The Sox also recalled left-handed pitcher <b>Brandon Eisert </b>from Triple-A Charlotte, optioning fellow lefty <b>Tyler Schweitzer </b>to Charlotte. Eisert, who made a pair of appearances with the Sox earlier this season and allowed four runs in 2„ innings, had a 5.79 ERA in 14 innings with Charlotte.</p><p>Schweitzer has a 9.00 ERA in four appearances for the Sox.</p><p><b>Getting healthier</b></p><p>Outfielders <b>Austin Hays </b>and <b>Everson Pereira </b>ran the bases Saturday and Venable said there are “really good indications” they are on the right path to getting back into the lineup.</p><p>“When you get out on the bases, that is kind of the precursor to going out on [a rehab] assignment,” Venable said. “Those guys are going to have to do it a couple of days here and then see where they’re at.”</p><p>Hays (left calf strain) has been on the injured list since May 4. With a right pectoral strain, Pereira is progressing but needs to prove he can throw.</p><p>“Throwing is the thing for him,” Venable said of Pereira, who was put on the IL on April 29. “He’ll have some other hurdles to clear here, but certainly he’s got his feet underneath him. He’s doing a great job.”</p><p><b>O’Nora injured</b></p><p>Home plate umpire <b>Brian O’Nora</b> left the game during the bottom of the fourth. Sox right fielder <b>Jarred Kelenic</b> fouled a <b>Jameson Taillon</b> pitch off O’Nora’s mask and near his jaw. O’Nora went down to a knee and was helped up by Cubs catcher <b>Miguel Amaya</b>. Following a delay, the game continued with <b>Erich Bacchus</b> behind home plate. Bacchus moved from second base, leaving the crew one umpire short.<br></p>
